Q: Azure DevOps Test Execution in DevOps A:

From my experience, the short answer is exactly what you described in your third bullet point (sorry). Azure DevOps adds a little bit of sugar to this setup by allowing you to create « requirements-based test suites » in your test plan. In that case, you do not have to manually add each new test case to your test suite but ADO automatically adds them as you create new test cases linked to your user stories. The test suite also automatically uses the ID and user story title in the title of the test suite.

You can add a bit more convenience to this but adding the test cases directly from the « Boards » view. I.e., you can add new test cases to your user stories by using the overflow menu on the card of a user story (I.e., without even having to open the user story’s work item form). From the same Boards view, you can then also directly execute your test points and set them to « passed » or « failed » (again, without having to open additional forms or even opening the Test plans module).

To view the test stats per user story, you would then have to use the « Reporting » page of the test plan from where you can filter for the test suite of said user story and then see executions statistics for it.

I think what you are describing in your second bullet point is not possible because a test point is always linked to a single test suite, which must be in a test plan. There is no globally accessible table to show you test results for all tests linked to a user story (maybe you could get there using Power BI and ADO’s Odata APIs but it would be non-trivial exercise). The closest you could get to this would be if you followed the above steps and only used a single test plan for all your tests in your project. That way, all your test execution statistics would be accessible in a single (potentially very large) test plans reporting page.

There could be an extension for this (or you could build one). But I have not checked.

Q: Postman "Directory Already Linked" error on new repo and workspace A:

I had this same issue. I was attempting to add a Git repo to a new workspace in Postman and my coworker had already created a workspace linked to the same Git repo. We're both members of the same Postman team (although I'm not sure if that last part matters).

The solution was for him to add me to the workspace. Whoever has already linked the repo to a workspace in Postman should do the following:

  1. In the workspace dropdown in Postman - click View all workspaces

  2. Choose the workspace you want to add a user to

  3. Under the Settings tab, click Manage People

  4. Invite someone and set their permission level

Alternatively, the person who has linked the git repo to the workspace can Disconnect the workspace from the git repo by doing the following:

  1. Select the workspace from the workspace dropdown in postman

  2. Click Local Files (file icon)

  3. In the ellipsis menu (...) choose Disconnect

The "Directory Already Linked" error was not clear. I thought I had already linked it myself and couldn't figure out how to unlink. I even deleted the workspace entirely, uninstalled and reinstalled Postman and saw the same error.

Q: Azure Blob Storage A:

I see. Well that is very bad... In our case, many users having many project with many files that are all likely large media files, such as .wav, makes me feel uneasy having them all in the same container. It sounds like there will be a direct correlation between users uploading files and reduced speed of queries for their files.

Is there some way to avoid this, like maybe a way to narrow the list parameters? As of now it looks like we are just listing all files in the container, and from the Rust API I don't currently see any other way to query for files but perhaps this is just a limitation of the Rust library.

Q: Where is the post featured image link stored in the WordPress database? A:

The other answers are correct, but I always come back here to reference the sql and have to adapt it and fix the formatting. Here is the sql that I normally use for this query:

SELECT m2.meta_value
FROM wp_posts p
INNER JOIN wp_postmeta m
    ON p.ID = m.post_id AND m.meta_key = '_thumbnail_id'
INNER JOIN wp_posts a
    ON m.meta_value = a.ID AND a.post_type = 'attachment'
INNER JOIN wp_postmeta m2
    ON a.ID = m2.post_id AND m2.meta_key = '_wp_attached_file'
